newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Rubbish dump makes Austrian village filthy rich.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rubbish dump makes Austrian village filthy rich.

text.p: A rubbish dump on the doorstep is not everyone's idea of a gold mine but one Austrian village has gone from rags to riches by turning litter into glitter.

Frohnleiten, a sleepy market town, has used huge profits from charges for use of its waste burial site to add sparkle to the lives of villagers by providing a wealth of services from a kindergarten to holidays for pensioners.
The only claim to fame of this community of 7,300 perched high on the banks of the River Mur in Austria's second-poorest province of Styria used to be its award-winning flowers.
But all that changed in 1987 when Frohnleiten became home to the waste site, grabbing the chance to mine an untapped gold vein when other villages turned up their noses.
The site became a moneyspinner and Frohnleiten is now the richest community in the province.

The market town silenced environmentalists by hermetically sealing the pit below the ground. And the site has regurgitated so much money that the initial start-up cost of 100 million schillings ($9.41 million) has brought many benefits to the community.
The busy road through the heart of this former Roman outpost was rerouted to create a pedestrian zone, and a state-of-the art subterranean garage provides free parking.
The community, largely employed in farming or forestry, now boasts a swish country hotel complete with private brewery, and council housing has been financed including a large convalescence home.

Each new-born child receives a savings account with 2,000 schillings, topped up with another 2,000 schillings for every milk tooth pulled. And for each child in kindergarten, the community donates 3,000 schillings a year.
The elderly and minimum wage earners are equally well provided for with contributions towards utility bills. People building their own houses receive a lump 50,000 schillings.
And those caught short have also not been forgotten.

For the price of just one schilling, you can spend a soothing 20 minutes listening to Strauss's Blue Danube waltz while relieving yourself in the self-cleaning toilet, a public facility which cost a hefty 900,000 schillings.

In fact the rubbish dump has made Frohnleiten so stinking rich that for a while the council seriously considered installing underground heating to prevent the pavements from icing over during Austria's long, cold winters.
"It's like living in an ideal world," said housewife Margarete Urban. "Everyone's well provided for, there's no crime -- no one even steals the flowers."
The dump, nestled high up in a deep and densely-wooded valley, buries 1,000 tonnes a day of non-biological waste from all over the country, the bulk of it packaging material.
On arrival, the first thing you notice are the pristine surroundings devoid of rubbish and any accompanying smells.

"We scoop out the innards of the mountain, seal the ground with a non-degradable cover, pack the rubbish in terraces, put another cover on top, then pile the earth back on and reforest it," said Josef Herler, the site foreman.

Pipes are threaded throughout the rubbish to catch escaping toxic water and gas. The water is delivered to a local water-purification plant while the methane gas is burnt off on-site. The rubbish itself eventually becomes a harmless mass.

"If ever there's such a thing as an environmentally-sound way to dispose of rubbish, then a burying facility like the one in Frohnleiten wins hands down over any incineration plant," said Wolfgang Pekny of the environmental group Greenpeace in Vienna.

"But the problem is there wasn't such a thing as a safe dump before 1990 when tighter regulations were enforced. Before you could chuck in any old rubbish, so, although the current management (at Frohnleiten) tries very hard, you don't know what's lurking at the very bottom of the dump," Pekny said.
A waste expert at an Austrian environmental group said the Frohnleiten plant was not an issue of concern.
Site foreman Herler said that the land, bought from three farmers, is filled close to capacity with garbage but that the community has purchased a further, albeit final, hunk of the mountain.
Then what?
"When we can dump no more here, we'll just have to pack up and move on to another mountain. There are plenty around," said Herler. ($1=10.63 Schilling)
